content_voiceover: This is the flow cytometry from an affected patient, and the contrast with the normal control is the key teaching point. GPIIb, CD41, is only forty percent positive instead of one hundred percent, GPIIIa, CD61, is only twenty-nine percent, and critically the dual-positive GPIIb-IIIa complex is just seven point two percent, far below normal. This markedly reduced surface expression of the fibrinogen receptor is the diagnostic hallmark of Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Functionally, PAC-1 binding also fails to activate appropriately, rising only from two point nine percent at baseline to fourteen point three percent after five micromolar ADP, nowhere near the ninety percent plus response seen in the normal control. This combination, absent or severely reduced GPIIb-IIIa expression plus failure of agonist-induced activation, confirms Glanzmann thrombasthenia. For boards, remember these patients have a normal platelet count and normal platelet morphology, but absent aggregation to all agonists except ristocetin, which distinguishes it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome where ristocetin-induced aggregation is also absent.
keypoints: GPIIb 40%, GPIIIa 29%, dual GPIIb/IIIa complex only 7.2%
Normal platelet count/morphology, aggregation absent except to ristocetin
keypoint_voiceover: This patient shows markedly reduced GPIIb and GPIIIa expression, with the dual-positive complex down to just seven percent of normal. PAC-1 activation is also blunted, rising only to fourteen percent after ADP stimulation compared to over ninety percent in a normal control. This pattern of low receptor expression with failed activation is diagnostic of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a disorder with normal platelet count but absent aggregation to all agonists except ristocetin.
